title: I Don't Want to Be the Difficult Friend
intro: Your friends choose a restaurant where you don't feel comfortable eating. You don't want everyone to change plans because of you.

content_body.prompt: What feels right for this situation?
content_body.review_note: This scenario translates teen lived experience into educational/self-management content. Keep it flagged for expert review before public release.

choices.label: Suggest one or two alternatives.
Eat beforehand or use a backup and still join them.
Ask everyone to help find somewhere that works.
Decide based on how much energy you have today.

by_choice_id.A: Your needs can be part of the group's planning.
by_choice_id.B: That may work when the social part matters most to you.
by_choice_id.C: You don't have to carry all the planning yourself.
by_choice_id.D: Your strategy doesn't have to be identical every time.

teaching_point: Your needs deserve consideration, and you get to decide how much energy you want to spend on a particular situation.
source_organization: Teen lived-experience synthesis; expert review required

title: Everyone Always Chooses Where I Can Eat
intro: A friend says, “Let's just go wherever you can eat.” Instead of feeling relieved, you feel guilty.

content_body.prompt: What's closest to what you're feeling?
content_body.review_note: This scenario translates teen lived experience into educational/self-management content. Keep it flagged for expert review before public release.

choices.label: I appreciate them, but I feel guilty.
I'm tired of being the reason.
I'm glad they want me included.
It's complicated—I feel more than one of these.

by_choice_id.A: It's possible to appreciate accommodation and still have complicated feelings about needing it.
by_choice_id.B: That feeling can be real even when your friends genuinely want you included.
by_choice_id.D: More than one feeling can be true at the same time.

teaching_point: Being included isn't the same as being a burden.
source_organization: Teen lived-experience synthesis; expert review required

title: I'm Tired of Bringing My Own Food
intro: You've brought your own food to events for years. You're tired of it.

content_body.review_note: This scenario translates teen lived experience into educational/self-management content. Keep it flagged for expert review before public release.

choices.label: I want to eat with everyone.
I mostly want to be there.
I want other people to help plan.
I have zero energy for this today.

by_choice_id.A: You might explore whether there's an option you feel comfortable with.
by_choice_id.B: Eating beforehand may be a reasonable strategy for you.
by_choice_id.C: You can practice asking others to share the planning work.
by_choice_id.D: A low-effort plan can still be good self-management.

teaching_point: Good self-management doesn't have to look identical every time.
source_organization: Teen lived-experience synthesis; expert review required

title: Why Can't We Just Be Spontaneous?
intro: School ends and friends say, “Let's go get food!” Nobody has picked a place.

content_body.review_note: This scenario translates teen lived experience into educational/self-management content. Keep it flagged for expert review before public release.

choices.label: QUICK: Suggest one of your known places.
EXPLORE: Help find somewhere new and do a focused check.
BACKUP: Use food you already have and join socially.
TOGETHER: Ask the group to help find somewhere workable.

by_choice_id.A: A trusted option can keep the plan moving.
by_choice_id.B: Trying a new option can be reasonable when you have the time and energy to assess it.
by_choice_id.C: You can preserve the social part without making food the whole event.
by_choice_id.D: Spontaneity doesn't mean you have to do all the planning.

teaching_point: Spontaneity with celiac may sometimes mean having flexible strategies—not having zero planning.
source_organization: Teen lived-experience synthesis; expert review required

title: I'm Just Tired of Thinking About Celiac
intro: You've been checking, researching, explaining and planning for a long time. Today you're simply tired of thinking about it.

content_body.prompt: What would help most right now?
content_body.review_note: This scenario translates teen lived experience into educational/self-management content. Keep it flagged for expert review before public release.

choices.label: Make the decision simpler.
Use something I already trust.
Ask someone to help.
Take a break from dealing with food if I can.
I'm not sure—I just want someone to get it.

by_choice_id.A: Using a familiar or low-effort option can reduce the mental load.
by_choice_id.B: You don't always have to investigate something new.
by_choice_id.C: Support can include sharing the planning work.
by_choice_id.D: Sometimes the social activity matters more than solving a food problem right now.

teaching_point: Knowing what to do doesn't mean it never gets exhausting. Reducing the mental workload can itself be useful.
source_organization: Teen lived-experience synthesis; expert review required

title: It's Gluten-Free, But I Don't Feel Safe
intro: You're told several dishes are gluten-free, but you don't know enough about how they were prepared.

content_body.review_note: This scenario translates teen lived experience into educational/self-management content. Keep it flagged for expert review before public release.

choices.label: Ask a few focused questions.
Look for packaged or separate options.
Decide not to eat.
Use something you brought or eat later.

by_choice_id.A: That may give you the missing information.
by_choice_id.B: That may reduce uncertainty about ingredients and handling.
by_choice_id.C: You are allowed to decide you don't have enough information or don't feel comfortable.
by_choice_id.D: A backup is another valid strategy.

teaching_point: “The ingredients are gluten-free” and “I have enough information to feel comfortable eating this” aren't always the same decision.
source_organization: Beyond Celiac cross-contact guidance; teen lived-experience extension

title: The Host Keeps Trying to Feed Me
intro: You decide not to eat. The host notices and says, “Oh no! Is there nothing you like? Let me find you something!”

content_body.review_note: This scenario translates teen lived experience into educational/self-management content. Keep it flagged for expert review before public release.

choices.label: Thank you so much. It's not that I don't like it—I just have to be careful about how food is prepared.
I'm totally okay. Please don't worry about me. I'm having a good time.
Could I see the package or ask how this was made?

by_choice_id.A: This explains the situation without criticizing the host.
by_choice_id.B: You can reassure the host and keep the focus on being together.
by_choice_id.C: If you want more information, it's reasonable to ask.

teaching_point: You can appreciate someone's hospitality without feeling obligated to eat.
source_organization: Teen lived-experience synthesis; expert review required

title: Everyone Says It's Fine
intro: Friends tell you, “Everyone said it's gluten-free. You're fine!” But nobody actually knows how it was prepared.

content_body.prompt: What information would help you decide?
content_body.review_note: This scenario translates teen lived experience into educational/self-management content. Keep it flagged for expert review before public release.

choices.label: Who made it and what ingredients were used?
How was it prepared and served?
Whether there is packaging or another reliable source of information.
Any combination of these.

by_choice_id.A: Knowing the source and ingredients can help.
by_choice_id.B: Preparation and serving can matter for cross-contact.
by_choice_id.C: A label or direct source may reduce uncertainty.
by_choice_id.D: Exactly. Your decision can be based on the information relevant to the situation.

teaching_point: Reassurance and information aren't the same thing.

title: I Asked Everything—and I'm Still Nervous
intro: You asked about ingredients and preparation and received answers. You still feel uneasy.

content_body.review_note: This scenario translates teen lived experience into educational/self-management content. Keep it flagged for expert review before public release.

choices.label: I need another piece of information.
I have enough information, but I'm still nervous.
I'd rather choose something else.
I don't want to eat right now.
I'm not sure.

by_choice_id.A: If something specific is unanswered, you can identify and ask about it.
by_choice_id.B: Sometimes the information question and the feeling question are different.
by_choice_id.C: You can make a different choice even after asking questions.
by_choice_id.D: You don't have to override discomfort to complete the situation.
by_choice_id.E: It's okay not to have an immediate answer.

teaching_point: Plan My C-Day helps you notice whether you're missing information, experiencing uncertainty, or choosing not to eat. It does not decide whether you should eat something.
source_organization: Teen lived-experience synthesis; expert review required

title: Food I Used to Love Looks Gross Now
intro: A year ago, a croissant might have looked delicious. Now it may look unappealing, unsafe, or completely different from how you remember it.

content_body.prompt: Does any of this sound familiar?
content_body.review_note: This scenario translates teen lived experience into educational/self-management content. Keep it flagged for expert review before public release.
content_body.clinical_safety_note: Do not frame the goal as overcoming disgust or persuading the teen to eat. If food-related fear/avoidance substantially interferes with eating or causes significant distress, the app may gently suggest talking with a parent/caregiver and the teen's celiac healthcare team.

choices.label: Foods with gluten don't appeal to me anymore.
They actually look gross to me.
Cross-contact worries me more than the gluten food itself.
Eating around gluten changes how I feel.
Not really.

by_choice_id.A: You don't need to want foods that contain gluten.
by_choice_id.B: Your feelings about foods can change after diagnosis.
by_choice_id.C: That distinction can be useful to notice.
by_choice_id.D: Food environments can carry new meaning after diagnosis.
by_choice_id.E: That's okay too. People adjust differently.

teaching_point: Your relationship with food can feel different after a major dietary change. What matters is having enough foods you can enjoy and support for managing celiac.
source_organization: Teen lived-experience synthesis; clinical review required

title: Going Somewhere Without Mom or Dad
intro: You're going on an outing without the person who usually helps ask food questions.

content_body.prompt: What could help you feel ready?
content_body.review_note: This scenario translates teen lived experience into educational/self-management content. Keep it flagged for expert review before public release.

choices.label: Research one or two options.
Save the questions you want to ask.
Bring a backup.
Ask for help if you need it.
Combine these.

by_choice_id.A: A little preparation can increase independence.
by_choice_id.B: Having your own script can make speaking up easier.
by_choice_id.C: Independence can include preparing for uncertainty.
by_choice_id.D: Being independent doesn't mean refusing support.
by_choice_id.E: You can build a plan that fits the situation.

teaching_point: Independence doesn't mean never needing support. It means building the skills to make more of your own decisions.
source_organization: Meyer & Naveh self-management framework; expert review required

title: My Friend Wants to Help
intro: A close friend asks, “What can I actually do that makes this easier for you?”

content_body.review_note: This scenario translates teen lived experience into educational/self-management content. Keep it flagged for expert review before public release.

choices.label: Help me check places before we go.
Don't make a big deal if I don't eat.
Ask me rather than assuming what's safe.
Learn what cross-contact means.
Honestly, just treat it normally.

by_choice_id.A: Sharing the planning work can help.
by_choice_id.B: Support can mean keeping the social situation comfortable.
by_choice_id.C: Letting you make the final decision respects your independence.
by_choice_id.D: A friend who understands the basics may be more helpful.
by_choice_id.E: Sometimes normalcy is the support you want.

teaching_point: Support doesn't have to come only from adults. You can tell friends what actually helps.
source_organization: Teen lived-experience synthesis; expert review required

title: Make School Better
intro: School events regularly include food but rarely give students with celiac enough information to plan.

content_body.review_note: This scenario translates teen lived experience into educational/self-management content. Keep it flagged for expert review before public release.

choices.label: Talk with a teacher or advisor.
Suggest that food information be shared beforehand.
Ask whether packaged GF options could be available.
Work with other students to suggest improvements.
Decide this isn't something you want to take on right now.

by_choice_id.A: Starting with one supportive adult may help.
by_choice_id.B: A small systems change could make planning easier.
by_choice_id.C: A concrete suggestion may be easier to act on.
by_choice_id.E: Having celiac does not obligate you to become an advocate.

teaching_point: Advocacy is an option—not another obligation created by having celiac.
source_organization: Expert review required; teen self-management extension

title: Correct the Myth—or Let It Go?
intro: Someone says, “Gluten-free is basically just a diet trend.”

content_body.prompt: What do you want to do?
content_body.review_note: This scenario translates teen lived experience into educational/self-management content. Keep it flagged for expert review before public release.

choices.label: Explain briefly that celiac disease is an autoimmune disease.
Say, “It's actually medically necessary for me,” and move on.
Don't engage.
Share an expert resource if they're genuinely interested.

by_choice_id.A: A short factual correction can be enough.
by_choice_id.B: You can correct the part that affects you without giving a lecture.
by_choice_id.C: You are not responsible for educating everyone.
by_choice_id.D: A trusted resource can be useful when someone wants to learn.

teaching_point: Advocacy includes deciding when you want to educate someone—and when you don't.

title: Help a Newly Diagnosed Teen
intro: A younger teen tells you, “I was just diagnosed. I feel like I'm never going to be able to do anything normally again.”

content_body.prompt: What might you want them to know?
content_body.review_note: This scenario translates teen lived experience into educational/self-management content. Keep it flagged for expert review before public release.

choices.label: It gets easier as you learn what works for you.
You don't have to figure everything out immediately.
Ask for help. You don't have to do this alone.
You'll find your own ways of handling social situations.
Some parts can still be hard—and that's okay to talk about.

by_choice_id.A: Your lived experience may offer hope without pretending everything is easy.
by_choice_id.D: There isn't one perfect way to live with celiac.

teaching_point: Lived experience can become a source of support for someone else. What do you wish someone had told you?
source_organization: Teen lived-experience synthesis; expert review required

title: I Think I Already Ate Gluten
intro: After eating, you realize the food may have contained gluten.

content_body.prompt: What do you need right now?
content_body.programming_rule: Do not provide medication, dosing, detoxification, or exposure-treatment instructions. This scenario requires clinical review before public release.

choices.label: Pause and avoid blaming yourself.
Tell a parent/caregiver or trusted adult if appropriate.
Follow the care guidance you already have from your healthcare team.
Seek appropriate medical care if you are seriously unwell.
Later, reflect on what information might help next time.

by_choice_id.A: Mistakes and uncertain situations can happen. Focus on what you need now.
by_choice_id.B: Support can be useful, especially if you feel unwell or unsure what to do.
by_choice_id.C: Plan My C-Day should not create a new treatment plan for an exposure.
by_choice_id.D: For urgent or severe symptoms, use appropriate medical/emergency care rather than relying on the app.
by_choice_id.E: Reflection can help future planning without turning the event into blame.

teaching_point: Focus on support, existing care guidance, and learning—not blame or a treatment algorithm.
